title: Committee for Economic Development Founded: Corporate Policy Network Established
description: The Committee for Economic Development (CED) is founded by Paul G. Hoffman (Studebaker Corporation president), William Benton (Benton & Bowles advertising co-founder), and Marion B. Folsom (Eastman Kodak treasurer) with backing from the U.S. Commerce Department. CED establishes 3,000 local committees enlisting 60,000 business leaders nationwide to shape post-war economic policy. Unlike the ultra-conservative National Association of Manufacturers, CED represents 'moderate-conservative' corporate interests willing to work with government. The organization becomes instrumental in creating the Bretton Woods Agreement, Employment Act of 1946, and Marshall Plan. CED establishes the model for corporate policy influence that later evolves into the Business Roundtable (1972), demonstrating how corporate interests organized sophisticated policy networks decades before the Powell Memo. This moderate business approach provides political cover for broader corporate agenda while maintaining influence over Democratic and Republican administrations.

sources.title: When 'Liberal' and 'Business' Belonged in the Same Sentence

significance: Establishes precedent for 'moderate' corporate policy organizations that provide political legitimacy while advancing business interests across party lines. CED's 60,000-member network demonstrates scale of corporate political organization already in place by 1942, predating the Powell Memo by 29 years. The organization's role in shaping major post-war policies (Bretton Woods, Marshall Plan, Employment Act of 1946) shows corporate influence embedded in policy formation from the outset.
